lines.title: Intro
lines.text: Hey, I'm Taylor. I'm a real human.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: I'm also a user experience and product designer, and I'd like to show you something I've been working on.

lines.title: Intro
lines.text: It's called Color Taylor.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I've always struggled with mixing colors using RGB. It turned out hue and saturation models were helpful for finding the colors that I want.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Let's say I have this turquoise color, but I want to get to teal, which is darker and more colorful. How do I dial that into the RGB?

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I think I need to lower red and blue,

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: but how much do I change the RGB before the color becomes unfamiliar?

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Once I understood how hue models and RGB work together, I could more confidently understand how colors were constructed. That made it easier to choose harmonious colors, which I could then build into larger systems.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Our focus for this presentation will be hue, saturation, and brightness.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: But the app supports HSL as well, so you can use what's familiar to you.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: Color Taylor is meant to be a playground and educational tool for how RGB and HSB work together.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: You see the relationships in real time, to help better understand how colors work on your display.

lines.title: Thesis
lines.text: I'll just move myself out of the way, for now.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: The color editor on the right should be familiar to most people who have worked with creative tools.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: The hexagon on the left is a different way of displaying the same information.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: Around the hex we have the Hue,

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: which is an angle that ranges from 0 to 360 degrees.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: Red is 0...

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: green is 120...

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: and blue is 240.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: By laying the primary colors out like this,

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: we can more easily see how RGB values determine a color's hue.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: You'll notice, between each of the primary colors we see combinations:

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: yellow, which is red and green combined;

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: cyan, which is green and blue;

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: and magenta, which is blue and red.

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: This Yellow, Cyan, and Magenta are not to be confused with CMYK,

lines.title: The hex and hue
lines.text: which is a larger topic for another time.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: Let's use an orangey color as a reference point,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: here at 30 degrees.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: Around 30 degrees we'll always have this warm tone between red and yellow.

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: At the highest saturation and brightness the color will be a combination of

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 2 parts red,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 1 part green,

lines.title: Orange at 30
lines.text: 0 parts blue.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Adding saturation increases the range between red, green, and blue.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Desaturating reduces the range proportionally between these.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Saturation scales off the highest value.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: In this case Red holds still.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Green and blue move toward it or away from it.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: When all three are equal, there's no saturation, and you're left with gray.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Notice the hue didn't change, we're still at 30, which is the same orangey source color we started with.

lines.title: Saturation
lines.text: Same hue, only the range between RGB values changed.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Brightness is determined by the highest RGB value.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: As we adjust the brightness, the hue and saturation are maintained by scaling the RGB values proportionately to each other.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Brightness scales off of zero. All three channels scale together, so the ratios between them stay the same.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: At a hundred percent brightness the hex is at its largest,

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: and lowering it shrinks the size of the hex.

lines.title: Brightness
lines.text: Notice we stay at the hue 30 orange while moving brightness.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We'll use the swatches section to show how we can use HSB to set six different variations of the same hue.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: We can use HSB to come up with a bright desaturated orange, then go down the scale until we have a dark vibrant variant.

lines.title: Six tints
lines.text: This is hinting at what a design system might do.

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: We've been exploring the playground, but if you want the classroom perspective, check out the equations section.

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: It shows the math behind

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: hue,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: saturation,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: brightness,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: and HSL conversions,

lines.title: Equations
lines.text: as well as how Hex and normalized colors are calculated.

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: Now we can move on to the demo, which gives you an outline of some of the things to look for in the Color Taylor app.

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: You can find this demo the first time loading the app,

lines.title: Handoff to the demo
lines.text: or from the question mark button at the top of the app.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Start with the sliders and controls you already know.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Moving one slider will highlight every other slider it affects.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the droplet button to switch between Source or Mixed colored sliders.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Click the tags button to show HTML colors on the hex.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Drag a handle on the hex and watch the RGB and HSB sliders follow.

lines.title: The demo
lines.text: Having fun is the goal of the tool.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If you use Figma, I've also made a Color Taylor plugin that you might like to check out.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: That's Color Taylor!

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Go play with it, and I hope it helps you see the relationship between RGB and HSB in a different light.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: If it's useful, I'd like to hear from you. Questions and feedback are welcome.

lines.title: Sign-off
lines.text: Thanks, see ya.
